etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English scheden, schede, from Old English scēadan, scādan (“to separate, divide, part, make a line of separation between; remove from association or companionship; distinguish, discriminate, decide, determine, appoint; shatter, shed; expound; decree; write down; differ”), from Proto-West Germanic *skaiþan, from Proto-Germanic *skaiþaną (compare West Frisian skiede, Dutch and German scheiden), from Proto-Indo-European *skeyt- (“to cut, part, divide, separate”), from *skey-.

See also Welsh chwydu (“to break open”), Lithuanian skėsti (“to spread”), skíesti (“to separate”), Old Church Slavonic цѣдити (cěditi, “to filter, strain”), Ancient Greek σχίζω (skhízō, “to split”), Old Armenian ցտեմ (cʻtem, “to scratch”), Sanskrit च्यति (cyáti, “he cuts off”)). Related to shoad, shit, sheath.

definitions.definition: (transitive, obsolete, UK, dialectal) To part, separate or divide.

quote.text: If there be any thing that knitteth himself to the ilk middle point [of a circle], it is constrained into simplicity (that is to say, into unmovablity), and it ceaseth to be shed and to flit diversely.
The northern wind had shed the misty clouds from the sky;

quote.citation: 1635, "Sermon on Philippians III, 7, 8", in Select Practical Writings of David Dickson (1845), Volume 1, page 166 Internet Archive

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive) To part with, separate from, leave off; cast off, let fall, be divested of.

quote.citation: 1707, J[ohn] Mortimer, The Whole Art of Husbandry; or, The Way of Managing and Improving of Land. […], London:  […]  J[ohn] H[umphreys] for H[enry] Mortlock […], and J[onathan] Robinson […], →OCLC:
quote.text: White oats are apt to shed most as they lie, and black as they stand.

quote.citation: 2012 November 2, Ken Belson, New York Times, retrieved 2 November 2012:
quote.text: She called on all the marathoners to go to Staten Island to help with the clean-up effort and to bring the clothes they would have shed at the start to shelters or other places where displaced people were in need.

definitions.definition: (transitive, archaic) To pour; to make flow.

quote.citation: c. 1591–1595 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Romeo and Ivliet”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii]:
quote.text: Did Romeo's hand shed Tybalt's blood?

definitions.definition: (transitive) To allow to flow or fall.

quote.citation: 2023 November 1, Paul Clifton, “RAIB recommends actions to tackle leaves on the line”, in RAIL, number 995, page 10:
quote.text: The crash occurred in a steep-sided cutting lined with self-seeded deciduous trees that were shedding their leaves, following unusually heavy rain and high winds in the 12 hours beforehand.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To radiate, cast, give off (light).

quote.citation: 1829, Edgar Allan Poe, “Tamerlane”, in Al Aaraaf, Tamerlane and Minor Poems:
quote.text: What tho’ the moon—the white moonShed all the splendour of her noon,Her smile is chilly—and her beam,In that time of dreariness, will seem(So like you gather in your breath)A portrait taken after death.

definitions.definition: (obsolete, transitive) To pour forth, give off, impart.

quote.citation: 1526, [William Tyndale, transl.], The Newe Testamẽt […] (Tyndale Bible), [Worms, Germany: Peter Schöffer], →OCLC, Acts ij:
quote.text: Sence now that he by the right honde of god exalted is, and hath receaved off the father the promys off the holy goost, he hath sheed forthe that which ye nowe se and heare.

definitions.definition: (obsolete, intransitive) To fall in drops; to pour.
To sprinkle; to intersperse; to cover.

quote.text: Her hair  […]  is shed with gray.

definitions.definition: (weaving) To divide, as the warp threads, so as to form a shed, or passageway, for the shuttle.
(music, slang) Alternative form of woodshed

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English sched, schede, schad, from a combination of Old English scēada (“a parting of the hair, top of the head”) and Old English ġesċēad (“distinction, reason”).

definitions.definition: (weaving) An area between upper and lower warp yarns through which the weft is woven.
(obsolete) A distinction or dividing-line.
(obsolete) A parting in the hair.
(obsolete) The top of the head.
(obsolete) An area of land as distinguished from those around it.
(physics) A unit of area equivalent to 10−52 square meters; used in nuclear physics

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Dialectal variant of a specialized use of shade.

definitions.definition: A slight or temporary structure built to shade or shelter something; a structure usually open in front; an outbuilding; a hut.

quote.citation: 1941 June, “Notes and News: The Derelict Glyn Valley Tramway”, in Railway Magazine, pages 279–280:
quote.text: There are numerous sheds in the now grass-grown yard, most of which now house threshing machines and farm carts instead of locomotives and rolling stock, although [in] the roofs of some are gaping holes.

definitions.definition: A large temporary open structure for reception of goods.
(British, derogatory, informal) An automobile which is old, worn-out, slow, or otherwise of poor quality.
(British, rail transport, informal) A British Rail Class 66 locomotive.

quote.citation: 2000 December 11, Bruce Garbutt, “Re: DRS to Cardiff (was Re: Tractor via Eddiestown)”, in uk.railway‎[1] (Usenet):
quote.text: Never saw that but we did stand and watch a pair of Sheds (156 and 165) speed north on a loaded steel.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To place or allocate a vehicle, such as a locomotive, in or to a depot or shed.

quote.citation: 1944 January and February, W. McGowan Gradon, “Forres as a Railway Centre”, in Railway Magazine, page 23:
quote.text: On the Dava line, apart from the banking assistance given by the 4-4-0s, the traffic is handled by the standard class "5" 4-6-0s, known among the drivers as "Hikers"; these engines are shedded at Inverness and Perth.

quote.citation: 1961 May, Mark B. Warburton, “Yatton and its branches to Clevedon and Wells”, in Trains Illustrated, page 277:
quote.text: Three 14XX class 0-4-2Ts were allocated to Bath Road for the Clevedon branch and one was sub-shedded at Yatton for a week at a time, during which period it amassed an aggregate mileage of nearly 1,400 miles.

definitions.definition: (transitive, music) To woodshed.
